title: Can you structure these 9 growth case questions in two minutes each?
description: 9 growth case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, if you turn each growth goal into its drivers (more customers, keeping them longer, more revenue from each, or new sources) before you reach for ideas. Growth prompts are open by nature, which is exactly why structure matters. Here are nine from different industries: give yourself two minutes per prompt, sketch your buckets out loud, then open the model structure and look for what you missed.
body:
How to use this set

For each prompt, set a two-minute timer and do three things: draw three or four buckets that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, add two or three specifics under each, and say where you would start and why. Then open the model. Each model gives the buckets, where to start, and the trap most candidates fall into.

Most growth structures are versions of one equation: revenue = customers × revenue per customer, with customers split into winning new ones and keeping existing ones. The skill is translating that into the client's own words. "Reach, conversion, retention" fits a newspaper; "more gyms, more members per gym" fits a gym chain. If you need a refresher first, read how to structure a growth case.

1. How should a newspaper grow digital subscriptions?

Show a model structure
  • Reach: traffic from search, social and newsletters; new audiences and topics.
  • Conversion: paywall design, free trials and price; friction at sign-up.
  • Retention: reading habits, apps and bundles; the cancellation process and win-back offers.
  • Revenue per subscriber: tiers, family plans and add-ons; annual versus monthly billing.

Where to start: map the funnel and find the step with the biggest drop-off. Net growth can stall because fewer readers start, or because more leave.

The trap: listing marketing ideas (SEO, social, newsletters) without the reach, convert, retain funnel. Those are solutions, not drivers.

2. How can a university attract more international students?

Show a model structure
  • Markets: which countries have demand; competition from universities in other countries.
  • Offer: courses, fees and scholarships; rankings and graduate job prospects.
  • Recruitment: agents, partner institutions and digital marketing; conversion from offer to enrolment.
  • Barriers: visa rules and policy; housing and student support.

Where to start: conversion from offer to arrival. Many offers are lost to visa problems and competing universities after the hard work of attracting an applicant is done.

The trap: ignoring visas and housing, which often cap numbers whatever the marketing budget.

3. How can a gym chain grow revenue by 20% in three years?

Show a model structure
  • More gyms: new sites; which cities and neighbourhoods.
  • More members per gym: conversion from trials and tours; new segments such as corporate, off-peak and older members.
  • Keep members longer: churn by month of membership; onboarding, classes and community.
  • More per member: price and premium tiers; personal training, retail and apps.

Where to start: keeping members longer. Churn is usually the biggest lever in gyms, and it costs less to keep a member than to win one. Note the target is only about 6% a year (1.2 to the power of one third), so it may not need new sites at all.

The trap: only thinking about new members.

4. How can a mobile operator increase revenue per customer?

Show a model structure
  • Price: plan prices and annual rises; fewer discounts on renewal.
  • Upgrade: bigger data plans and 5G; handset financing.
  • Add services: insurance, streaming bundles and home broadband; family plans.
  • Protect value: churn among high-value customers; customers moving down to cheaper plans.

Where to start: upgrades and added services. Price rises are fastest but risk churn in a market where switching is easy.

The trap: raising prices without checking what happens to churn.

5. Should a bubble-tea chain grow by franchising instead of opening its own shops?

Show a model structure
  • Economics for us: fees and royalties versus own-shop profits; capital needed each way.
  • Speed: shops opened per year under each model; our capacity to manage growth.
  • Control: quality and brand consistency; choosing and supporting franchisees.
  • Economics for franchisees: the franchisee's payback; whether good partners will sign up.

Where to start: economics for franchisees. If they cannot make money, the model fails however good the royalty looks.

The trap: looking only at our royalty income.

6. How can a national museum raise $10M a year more without charging for entry?

Show a model structure
  • Visitors: more visits and longer stays; tourists versus locals.
  • Spend per visitor: shop, café and paid exhibitions; donations at the door.
  • Other income: events and venue hire; licensing images and touring exhibitions.
  • Supporters: memberships and patrons; corporate partners and grants.

Where to start: paid exhibitions and events, which bring the largest sums quickly. Sanity-check each idea against the $10M target: an extra $2 of spend from 1M visitors is only $2M.

The trap: only thinking about the shop and café.

7. How can a coworking company double revenue in three years?

Show a model structure
  • More space: new buildings and partnerships with landlords; which cities.
  • Fuller space: occupancy; private offices versus desks; corporate teams.
  • Price: rates versus rivals; contract length.
  • More services: meeting rooms and events; virtual offices and add-ons.

Where to start: fuller space. Filling existing buildings costs far less than opening new ones. But doubling in three years needs about 26% growth a year, so occupancy alone will rarely be enough; expect new space to be part of the answer.

The trap: only opening new locations.

8. How can an airline raise extra revenue per passenger?

Show a model structure
  • Before the flight: bags, seats and priority boarding; fare bundles.
  • On board: food, drink and Wi-Fi; duty free.
  • Around the trip: hotels, car hire and insurance, earning commission from partners.
  • Loyalty: selling points to credit card partners; subscriptions.

Where to start: before the flight. Bags and seats are usually the largest source of extra revenue per passenger.

The trap: charging for everything and damaging customer satisfaction and repeat bookings.

9. How can a charity grow its donations by 30%?

Show a model structure
  • More donors: new audiences, digital and events; cost to acquire each donor.
  • Keep donors: monthly giving, thanking and reporting impact; why donors stop.
  • Bigger gifts: major donors and legacies; matched giving from employers.
  • Other sources: grants and corporate partners; trading and shops.

Where to start: keeping donors. Retaining a donor is usually far cheaper than finding a new one, and regular givers are worth more over time.

The trap: only running bigger campaigns.

How to score your answer

Take the newspaper prompt. A complete tree separates reach, conversion, retention and revenue per subscriber. A list of SEO, pricing and newsletters mixes drivers with solutions. Rewrite each branch as something you could measure before choosing an initiative.

The best first question is: "Has growth slowed because fewer readers subscribe, or because more cancel?" The numbers show why it matters. Suppose the paper has 100,000 subscribers, gains 4,000 a month and loses 3% a month. It loses 3,000, so it grows by 1,000 a month. If churn doubles to 6%, it loses 6,000 and shrinks by 2,000 a month, and no amount of extra traffic at the same conversion rate fixes that cheaply.

When you compare your structure with the model, mark three things: a missing driver, a branch that overlaps another, and a better first question. One corrected structure teaches more than ten you never look at again.
